# 杂项·其他 {.unnumbered}



> 本主题共 11 篇语境短文。每篇把一批旧词织进一个场景；目标词**加粗**，展开"本篇生词"可遮释义自测。



### Lost in the Archive

A researcher sorting through an **are**a of uncategorized files discovers a curious mix of the obscure and the mundane. The cabinet before her is labeled simply "**non**-standard terms" — a **bon** catch-all for anything that **was** too odd to shelve elsewhere. She pulls out a folder marked **UEE** and finds inside a single sticky note that reads, in faded pencil, *"**thy** guess is as good as mine."*

She moves to the next drawer: **PRE**-filed fragments. A slip of **chad** from an old punch-card machine sits beside a printout titled **SCI** Codes and a handwritten memo stamped **HOC**. Someone has scrawled the word **crap** across the top in red ink — a blunt editorial judgment that has survived at least three reorganizations. She sets it in the **bing** of paper to be reviewed later, a growing heap of material that nobody quite knows what to do with.

By the window, a technician consults a screen: **CAL**, **TTE**, **DET**, **PAG**, **POO**, **trt**, **sbs**, **CONS** — all abbreviations whose full forms live somewhere in a **San** Francisco warehouse along with the rest of the legacy documentation. He **quo**tes a line from the manual aloud, testing whether it still makes sense. It does not. He places the binder on the **tee** stand at the corner of his desk — a small platform someone 3D-printed specifically for binders nobody dares throw away.

Down the hall, an archivist of a more **desi**gnated kind handles the physical curiosities: a lump of **dag** wrapped in cloth, a jar labeled **CAUS** (Color Association of U.S., class of 1971), and a badge once belonging to a **beth** — a second-order clerk whose role no longer exists. She notes the items in the log with **AYES** checked under "retain," because the **cide** of any artifact, however minor, must be formally authorized. In the margin she draws a small **hoy** — a flat-bottomed boat she once saw on the river, which seemed to her the perfect symbol for things that carry a little of everything and belong to no particular shore.

### Odds, Ends, and a Few Regrets

The old neighborhood felt like the **dregs** of a city that had moved on without saying goodbye. On the corner, a **buzzy** neon sign flickered above a shop selling **dummy** replicas of vintage polo shirts — each one a **combi** of polyester and nostalgia. A kid outside, probably named **Chris** or **Ryan**, scrolled his phone and muttered "**aight**" to no one in particular, then typed "**LMAO**" and pocketed it.

Inside the café, a barista named **Avery** hummed to herself while grinding beans. She had pasted a handwritten quote from **Dante** above the espresso machine — something about descending, which felt appropriate. On the counter sat a battered paperback with **Enoch**'s name scrawled on the cover page, a sticky note reading "**syn.**" beside an underlined passage, as if the previous reader had been building a private glossary. Nearby, an **Avent** baby bottle stood next to a to-go cup — some parent's morning **combi** of competing demands.

A man who called himself **Cesar** — and who carried himself with the practiced authority that name implies — held court at the corner table. He had the **horny**-skinned hands of someone who had worked outdoors for decades, and the vocabulary of someone who had not. He referred to a former colleague as a "complete **turd**" and a local politician as a "**twat**," then caught himself, glanced at **Fanny** behind the register, and switched to Spanish: "**bueno**, forget I said that." He was reading about the **Hawks**' latest loss, annotating the box score the way **Engel** might annotate a cost curve — with grim precision. On his lapel, a small **ASTRO** mission patch sat crooked, a souvenir from a nephew who worked in aerospace. He'd once pulled a **boner** of his own in that world — misread a spec sheet, ordered the wrong fittings — and the story had followed him like the word "**slut**" follows certain women: unfairly, loudly, and long past its occasion.

Outside, **thee** old elm they'd planted in '89 still stood, indifferent. A crow on its highest branch opened its beak, as if it **doth** know something the rest of us do not. A bottle of **amara** tincture sat on the windowsill of the apartment above — someone's bitter cure for something unnamed. The crow watched, **Ryan** scrolled, **Avery** ground more beans. The city **LMAO**'d and moved on. **Yeap** — same as it ever was.

### Lost in the Archive Room

The old storage room was a genuine **trove** — **bubbly** excitement spread through the small team the moment they pulled open the door. Inside, a **bundle** of manila folders sat wedged between a cracked **candle** holder and a defunct **buffer** device left over from some long-dead server rack. The overhead light flickered, casting **loopy** shadows that made the space feel vaguely **potty**, as if the room itself had gone a little mad from decades of neglect.

**Keith** crouched near a dusty shelf and lifted a glass dome — a **bubble** of antique crystal that someone, maybe a collector named **Jared** or **Josue**, had tucked behind a stack of old **IELTS** prep books. A handwritten label on the spine read *Property of **Carlos** **Castro**, do not **cancel**.* Next to it lay a **diaper** bag, of all things, still tagged for a baby shower that was apparently never held. "**Busted**," muttered **Connor**, meaning the zipper, though the word fit the whole scene.

**Hsue** — the archivist everyone called **Hsiao** — had warned them the room was a mess, but this was something else. She found a battered tin printed with **cheesy** clip-art, stuffed with notes about a **monte** game someone had apparently run on Friday evenings. A faded **SAGES** operations manual sat beneath it, alongside a laminated card describing the **cutoff** dates for **Danite** genealogy records. The **debris** was not just physical — it was temporal, each layer a stratum of **one's** forgotten intentions.

The team from the **Hyatt** had sent a consultant, a real **buster** of a fixer type, to assess whether clearing the room was **doable** before the renovation. Standing in the doorway, he scanned the chaos from the **cradle** of the frame, said nothing for a long moment, and then announced that yes, it could be done — but they would need a proper plan, not some **cheesy** workaround. He pulled out his phone, opened an app, and got to work.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

### Odds, Ends, and a Very Strange Evening

The evening had started in **tandem** — two old friends walking side by side down a rain-slicked alley, a **magnum** of red wine tucked under one arm, a half-finished **parcel** of takeaway under the other. **Oliver** was the kind of man who wore **shades** even at dusk, convinced it made him look less like a **novice** and more like someone who had seen things. His companion, **Martha**, had found her **outlet** in archaeology: she could spend a weekend helping a crew **exhume** a medieval rubbish pit and call it a holiday.

The venue they stumbled into was a converted warehouse whose walls still bore the **groove** of old machinery. Someone had **tagged** every surface with spray paint — names, dates, fragments of verse that might have been **Hesiod** if Hesiod had owned a can of chrome silver. A **popper** near the entrance was handing out glow sticks with the solemn efficiency of a customs officer. In one corner a **sprite**-like woman in a **domino** mask was explaining the rules of floor **hockey** to a man who looked, inexplicably, like a nervous **Epirot** who had wandered in from a different century altogether. The night had all the hallmarks of a **fiasco**, and yet nobody left.

The DJ set that followed did not **fizzle** — it ignited. **Spooks** of coloured light played across the **flanks** of the crowd. A **leaked** set list pinned to a pillar named the headliner only as **Monroe**, though a **paster** sticker below had been amended in biro to read *Pilate washed his hands of this booking*. Someone invoking **Gloria** in the chorus got the whole room singing. It was the sort of night that historians — **Origen** perhaps, or even **Grimes** — might one day puzzle over, a scene so miscellaneous it resisted any single account, **GLORIA** and **sodomy** scandals and **natans** algae in the drainage ditch outside all somehow part of the same sprawling, unclassifiable human evening.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

### Lost in the Archive Room

The old researcher, a quiet man who had made it his life's work to chronicle miscellaneous discoveries, sat surrounded by **clutter** — stacked folders, broken **fixture**s, a cracked **urinal** basin someone had left in the corner as a joke. He was no **zombie**, shuffling through the mess without thought; he moved with purpose, however odd his surroundings. A dusty **coaster** beneath a coffee mug bore the faded name **Vivian**, a colleague long transferred away. Beside it lay a scrapbook labeled simply **Winnie**, stuffed with press clippings about a **debacle** that had nearly ended the department's funding three years prior.

He had been tasked with sorting the legacy files of **Thales**, the project's founding director, whose papers were hopelessly **clogged** with redundant drafts. Every page was a **trifle** in isolation — a footnote on **Truman**-era policy, a sketch of the **Tyburn** site pulled from a London archive, a blurry photo of the **Valdez** spill that **Alvarez** had annotated in red ink. The **deviser** of this filing system, whoever it was, deserved a monument to poor judgment. The researcher himself had committed one career **blunder** after another in this room: a **blooper** at the **Bradley** symposium, an ill-timed remark about **Bridget**'s methodology, a funding memo so badly **blended** with another project's numbers that the director, a stern woman named **Dorothy**, had asked him point-blank whether he was serious or merely **trifling**.

He found the **fortune** of a lifetime in the bottom drawer: a **vatage** ledger — incomplete, gloss-free, yet unmistakably signed **Anthony** — that scholars had assumed lost. He set it on the **cushion** of the reading chair, cleared the **garbage** off the side table, and thought of **Corinne** at the front desk, who would know exactly which archivist to call. **Vulcan** himself, the old myth said, forged order out of chaos. The researcher allowed himself a small, tired smile. He was no god — but he could, at least, clear the desk.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

### A Most Miscellaneous Museum Evening

The curator — a gaunt man everyone called **Gregory** — had built his career on a single **gimmick**: staging pregame receptions before each new exhibition opened, so that donors arrived already primed to open their wallets. Tonight, however, the **pregame** cocktail hour had gone sideways. A pipe near the roof was **leaking**, dripping onto a rare Persian rug whose deep crimson, woven by **Persian** craftsmen four centuries ago, was slowly blooming with dark stains. Gregory muttered something **grating** under his breath and called a **Siemens** facilities technician.

Meanwhile, the main hall offered a **mélange** of curiosities that no single theme could contain. A wall panel on **Permian** megafauna stood beside a placard about **Homo sapiens** — the label still read *sapiens* in italic print — and a glass case held actual **nuggets** of Klondike gold. Across the room, a child had been corralled inside a toddler **playpen** someone had dragged in for a school group; he was giving his older brother repeated **noogies**, which his mother, a woman named **Ophelia**, pretended not to see. A **remnant** of the school group's banner lay crumpled near the fire exit, a **sematic** yellow-and-black stripe warning visitors of the wet floor.

The evening lecture touched on everything and nothing: a **Semitic** script found etched on a Bronze Age jar; a **Pharaoh**'s copper drill-bit; a reconstruction of a **Martian** soil sample rack; the philosophy of **Spinoza** — his *materia* lectures displayed in facsimile alongside the original Latin. In the sports alcove, a **Raptors** jersey hung framed beside a **Molotov** cocktail bottle from a Cold War exhibit, which made at least one guest visibly uneasy. The **run-off** vote for "Exhibit of the Year" was still open on a tablet by the door — really a **playoff** in miniature, one **remnant** nomination facing another in a head-to-head **run-off**. A donor named **Maynard** leaned on the **playpen** railing, scrolling through **Scripps** research abstracts on his phone, looking deeply unbothered.

Outside, a **slapper** mechanism on the loading dock kept misfiring, sending a dull clang through the atrium every few minutes. Someone had stashed a tin of **hashish**-scented candles near the ventilation grate — unopened, thankfully — and a tattered **hammock** from a maritime display had been re-strung between two pillars by person or persons unknown. Gregory surveyed the whole spectacle: the leaking pipe, the preoccupied donors, the Spinoza facsimiles, the noogies, the hammock. He poured himself a second glass of wine and decided it was, on balance, a perfectly normal opening night.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

### Odds, Ends, and Everyone In Between

Perched on a **barstool** near the **doorstop**-propped entrance, the historian turned the **doorknob** of an old wooden **cabinets** unit and pulled out a thick folder. Inside were **strands** of mismatched notes — fragments on **Akkadian** clay tablets, a side-by-side comparison of **Tagalog** and Latin verb forms, and a half-finished essay on **Avicenna**'s influence on medieval medicine. He had been working through **tryouts** for a new research assistant, hoping to fill the **vacancy** left by his last colleague. So far, none of the candidates had impressed him. One had a history of **truancy** at seminars; another had suggested a **deletion** of the entire **Achilles**-myth chapter, which he flatly refused.

Outside, a **carousel** of campus life kept spinning. A **castaway** from the drama club — dismissed after a **blow out** rehearsal — sat quietly on a bench. Nearby, two students debated whether to **call off** a **billiard** tournament planned for the weekend, since the hall was still **confined** by renovation barriers. A loud voice called "**tallyho**!" from across the courtyard — someone's theatrical way of announcing they had spotted the dean. The **Cesarian**-themed float for the history parade rolled past, attended by a student dressed unconvincingly as **Cromwell**, another as **Benedict**, and a third as **Winston**, waving from a rickety **tournee** wagon.

Inside again, the historian sighed and began to **wind up** his notes for the day. His **Christie**-style mystery novel — a passion project — sat in a drawer, its protagonist a law clerk named **Courtney** who specialised in estates of the **decedent**. He had read somewhere that **billards** — an archaic spelling he loved — had once been played in the halls of **Avicenna**'s era. Probably apocryphal. He closed the folder, adjusted the **doorknob** latch, and stepped out into the cool afternoon.

### A Day of Odds and Ends

The morning after deciding to **sleep in**, **John Doe** — a perfectly ordinary man with no particular story — finally rolled out of bed and shuffled past the overflowing **dumpster** in the alley. Someone had tossed in a cracked **billiards** cue and, inexplicably, a jar of fake **emeralds**. He paused at the **threshold** of the building's back door, trying to make sense of it all, then shrugged and moved on.

Down at the community center, a **breakdown** of the week's events was posted on the bulletin board: a **lacrosse** demonstration had gone sideways when a stray ball knocked a **Phillips** screwdriver off a shelf and straight into the sound system, an **auxiliary** speaker included. The volunteer coordinator — a woman named **Jennifer**, who had read enough **herstory** to know that heroines rarely get credit — was already on the phone ordering a replacement **accessory** kit. **By chance**, **Theodore** from the philosophy club wandered in, muttering something about **Plotinus** and the nature of the One, while clutching a dog-eared paperback on **Voltaire** and a loose page of notes on **Polonius**. Nobody asked.

Outside, a kid in a **gertrude** onesie sat watching an older cousin **spice up** a dull afternoon by narrating a backyard game as though **Godzilla** were bearing down on the neighbourhood. His commentary was **well set** in the grand tradition of neighbourhood drama, somewhere between **Bonaparte**'s battle dispatches and a **Goldberg** deal gone loud. In the end, everything settled — not through any plan but simply because, as the evening light held, **there is** always a quiet moment that makes the whole messy day **accessory** to something almost pleasant.

### A Miscellany of Moments

The old reading room had a **Byzantine** filing system — drawers within drawers, cross-referenced by codes no one alive could fully decode. On the desk sat a worn paperback of **Descartes**, its spine cracked from years of **haphazard** thumbing. Beside it, a model **hatchback** in pale blue plastic, the kind you win at a school raffle, shared shelf space with a toy **limousine** missing one wheel. A **makeshift** stand fashioned from a binder clip kept them from rolling off.

The room's curator, old **Sebastian**, had an eye for the incidental. A **Methuselah** of the archive world, he'd outlasted three building renovations and one **fire alarm** that turned out to be a burnt sandwich. A framed photograph showed **Roosevelt** shaking hands with a man whose identity remained an **oversight** — no caption, no date. Next to it hung a tournament bracket for **backgammon**, signed by someone named **Robertson** and countersigned by **Tomlinson**. A **Hanoverian** coin and a **goldilocks** figurine with frizzy yellow hair completed the windowsill.

On a corkboard above the radiator, someone had pinned notes on **Anaxagoras**, **Democritus**, and **Heraclitus** — three philosophers whose disagreements, scrawled in red pen, still felt urgent. A **Lancaster** bomber profile was sketched in the margin of an **Egyptology** pamphlet. A sticky note read simply: **here we go**. The shelf below held a **perishable** items log from a long-defunct canteen, a spare **pillowcase** folded into quarters, a circuit-board **eliminator** whose purpose no one remembered, and a printout titled "Introduction to **hypervideo**." A single line at the bottom of the corkboard, written in pencil: *"**Mauy Thai** class moved to Thursday."* Whether that was a correction or a wish, the room declined to say. The whole arrangement was, in the end, perfectly **like-kind** — each oddity recognising itself in the next. Somewhere overhead, a **helicopter** passed, and Sebastian did not look up.

### Miscellany at the Museum of Odd Human Things

The exhibition hall was a **springboard** for the strangest collection imaginable. Under the **Hellenistic** marble archway, a placard quoted **Xenophanes** and **Anaximander** — pre-Socratic thinkers who would have found the displays utterly baffling. One glass case held a cracked tube of **toothpaste** beside a squeaky **Neanderthal** skull replica; **oddly enough**, they shared the same label: *"Tools of the Mouth."* A **Tamagotchi** sat in the next case, its battery long dead, next to a faded **diaper pail** — both monuments to the anxious labour of keeping something alive.

The gift shop was, of course, the real draw. **Afficianados** of the peculiar lined up to browse **collectible** pins and **convertible** tote bags that could fold into hats. A **firecracker** wrapper from a 1987 New Year was priced at forty dollars. The curator — who had somehow managed to **get away with** calling half the donations "art" — stood by the register looking smug. Someone whispered, "**The jig's up**," after spotting a **Sloth love Chunk** T-shirt marked as a "rare artefact." The **terminator**-themed corner featured chrome prosthetic hands beside earnest wall text on mythology and **fornication** in ancient Greece, which also touched on **cunnilingus** with a composure that would have made **Nightingale** herself raise an eyebrow.

A documentary looped on a small screen: circus performers launching off a **teeterboard**, NFL running back **Elbert 'Ickey' Woods** doing his famous shuffle, and a philosophical interlude on **pornography** in the digital age — costumes, contracts, **provisions** for performer safety, **you name it**. The final room was roped off with a sign that read *"**What a geek!**"* and *"**What a queer!**"* — reclaimed insults now framed in gold. A child tugged her father's sleeve. "**Be careful with** that," he said, as she reached toward the last exhibit: a **convertible** toy car, every panel **collectible** by design, still in its box, never opened.
